Spectators remember the final.

Nobody remembers the person standing by the touchline with a stopwatch in one hand, a scoresheet in the other and a ringing phone in their pocket.

Here is what their tournament actually consists of:

Two weeks before.

Forty messages about entries, half arriving the night before the deadline. Three versions of the schedule because two year groups cannot play on Tuesday. A negotiation with whoever normally has the hall at that time.

All of this before anyone touches a ball.

Match day.

A kid turns up without kit — you are digging through a cupboard five minutes before kickoff. A ball goes over the fence. A parent asks why their son is not starting.

And in parallel you are keeping score, because there is no secretary.

That evening.

An argument about who advanced from the group. You are doing goal difference in pen on the edge of the scoresheet while two coaches do it alongside you and get a different answer.

Because someone wrote 3:1 as 3:2 in round two.

That night.

Collating results from three sheets of paper and two blurry photos in a group chat. Report due at nine. Replies to parents.

Tomorrow you go to work and teach six lessons.

I am not writing this to sell anything.

We build a tool for this job, and the longer we build it the clearer it gets: most of the job is not about sport. It is about data, messaging and patience.

And it is completely invisible to everyone except the person doing it.

If you have ever run a tournament, tell me which part is yours.

Genuinely curious whether entries, scoring or the report hurts most.
